summary:
RedTrail is an interactive Mars exploration and route-planning application developed for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. Focused on the Jezero Crater region, it combines real Martian orbital imagery from the CTX instrument with elevation data from a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) to help users understand the terrain and plan routes across the Martian surface.

The application features an interactive map with coordinate navigation, elevation and slope analysis, and two route-planning options: the shortest traversable route and a terrain-aware alternative. By evaluating slope and terrain costs, RedTrail helps users compare routes and identify paths that may be more suitable for traversal, rather than relying solely on geographical distance.

This is important because navigating Mars presents challenges such as uneven terrain, steep slopes, and limited mobility. RedTrail aims to support better-informed exploration and mission-planning decisions by making Martian terrain data accessible, understandable, and actionable through an interactive mapping interface.
details:
RedTrail is an interactive Mars mapping and terrain-aware route-planning application specifically addressing the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. Focused on the Jezero Crater region, RedTrail transforms real Martian geographical data into an interactive environment where users can explore the surface, analyse terrain characteristics and plan alternative routes.

What does it do and how does it work?

RedTrail uses a 5 m/pixel CTX orthomosaic for surface imagery and a 20 m/pixel CTX Digital Elevation Model (DEM) to obtain elevation information. A slope raster is derived from the elevation data and used in terrain analysis.

Users can interact with the map, navigate using Mars coordinates, select starting and destination points, and calculate two different routes:

  • Shortest traversable route: Finds a route that minimises distance across valid terrain without applying an additional slope penalty.
  • Terrain-aware route: Incorporates slope penalties into route evaluation, potentially choosing a more suitable path over difficult terrain.

Users can compare the routes through distance, average and maximum slope, elevation gain, estimated travel time and terrain cost. A configurable maximum passable slope also allows users to exclude terrain exceeding a selected threshold. The application handles NoData regions so that invalid terrain information is not treated as valid ground.

What benefits does it have and what is its intended impact?

Mars presents significant navigation challenges due to uneven surfaces, elevation changes and potentially difficult slopes. RedTrail helps address these challenges by making terrain information accessible and allowing users to compare routes beyond geographical distance alone.

Its intended impact is to support better-informed surface exploration and mission-planning decisions. It provides a foundation for evaluating terrain, understanding potential navigation difficulties and identifying alternative paths for future rover and astronaut exploration missions.

What tools and technologies were used?

RedTrail was developed using JavaScript and Vite, with:

  • OpenLayers: Interactive map rendering and navigation.
  • GeoTIFF: Accessing and processing geospatial raster datasets.
  • Proj4: Implementing the custom Mars coordinate projection.
  • CTX orthomosaic and DEM datasets: Providing real Martian imagery and elevation information.
  • Browser-side processing: Loading raster data and generating map tiles without requiring a dedicated map-rendering backend at runtime.

The application is a software-based solution and does not currently require additional hardware.

How is the project creative and what factors did the team consider?

RedTrail's key innovation is its combination of real Martian imagery, elevation-derived slope analysis and comparative route planning in one interactive application. Instead of treating the shortest geographical path as automatically preferable, it evaluates terrain characteristics and allows users to understand the trade-offs between alternative routes.

During development, our team considered scientific data availability and resolution, coordinate accuracy, terrain passability, slope constraints, invalid or missing raster data, route distance, estimated traversal time and interface usability. We also considered the limitations of our assumptions, particularly that the slope threshold and estimated travel times are experimental and are not validated astronaut mobility limits.

Ultimately, RedTrail aims to turn complex planetary data into practical navigation insights, contributing to safer and more informed exploration of the Martian surface.
